thinkBeforeYouCode.question: Why must the filter parameter be Predicate<? super T> instead of Predicate<T>?
thinkBeforeYouCode.mentorInsight: PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. The filter is a CONSUMER of T (it reads T to make a decision). Using <? super T> allows a general predicate (like Predicate<AuditableEvent>) to filter a specific subtype (like PaymentTransaction) without compilation errors.

thinkBeforeYouCode.question: Why should the input collection be Iterable<? extends T> instead of Iterable<T>?
thinkBeforeYouCode.mentorInsight: The input collection is a PRODUCER of T (the pipeline reads elements from it). Generics are invariant: List<WirePayment> is NOT a List<Payment>. Using <? extends T> allows the pipeline to accept List<WirePayment> seamlessly.

thinkBeforeYouCode.question: How does PipelineResult maintain immutability of returned data?
thinkBeforeYouCode.mentorInsight: By wrapping results in List.copyOf(successes) and List.copyOf(failures), callers cannot alter the pipeline's internal state or compromise audit logs.

activities.title: Practical Context: Water Purification & Mineral Enrichment Plant
activities.description: How multi-stage filtering and transformation stages turn raw inputs into refined outputs.
activities.content:
Imagine an industrial water purification facility. Untreated raw water from various mountain reservoirs (Iterable<? extends RawWater>) enters the intake pipe.

The stream passes through several physical filter screens that remove sediment and impurities (Predicate<? super Water> filters). It then undergoes quality testing probes checking chemical and biological safety standards (Rule<? super Water>). Water that fails the safety standards is diverted into a quarantine tank with an incident log (ValidationFailure).

Water that passes all filters enters the mineralization chamber, which enriches the water and bottles it into premium mineral water (Function<? super Water, ? extends BottledProduct>). The pipeline operates generically regardless of which specific spring the water came from, delivering verified output and an auditable reject log.

activities.title: Architecture of a PECS-Compliant Generic Pipeline
activities.description: Technical analysis of PECS wildcard mechanics, contravariant consumers, and covariant producers.
activities.content:
### Formal Computer Science Definition
A generic pipeline is a composable higher-order stream processor that consumes an input sequence of upper-bounded type $\tau_{in} \le T$, applies a sequence of contravariant predicates $\phi: T \to \text{bool}$, and projects valid elements via a covariant morphism $f: T \to R$ into an immutable output sequence.

### The PECS Wildcard Map

```
                                Pipeline<T>
                                     |
     +-------------------------------+-------------------------------+
     |                                                               |
Input Producer (PECS: Extends)                             Rule Consumers (PECS: Super)
- Iterable<? extends T> items                              - Predicate<? super T> filter
- We READ from this collection                             - Rule<? super T> rule
- Accepts Subtype of T                                     - We PASS T into this consumer
                                                           - Accepts Supertype of T
                                     |
                    [Transformation: Function<? super T, ? extends R>]
                                     |
                             PipelineResult<R>
                    - List<R> successfulItems (immutable)
                    - List<ValidationFailure> failures (immutable)
```

### Critical Rules of Generics Design
1. **Consumer Super**: Any method that passes an element into a callback (`predicate.test(item)`, `consumer.accept(item)`) must declare `? super T`. This allows a general `Predicate<Object>` or `Predicate<Entity>` to validate a `User`.
2. **Producer Extends**: Any method that reads elements from a data source (`collection.iterator()`) must declare `? extends T`. This allows a `List<AdminUser>` to be passed to a method expecting `Iterable<User>`.

questions.question: Why does filter(Predicate<? super T> predicate) use '? super T' instead of 'T'?
options: It allows the JVM to allocate less heap memory
It enables a broader predicate defined on a supertype of T (such as Predicate<Object>) to filter elements of type T
It makes the filter execute on multiple CPU threads
It enforces that T implements Comparable
questions.explanation: Under PECS, a predicate consumes T. Declaring Predicate<? super T> allows any predicate that can handle a supertype of T to be used seamlessly.

questions.question: What is the consequence of declaring the input parameter as process(List<T> items) instead of process(Iterable<? extends T> items)?
options: The method cannot accept a List<SubtypeOfT> because generic types are invariant in Java
The method throws ClassCastException at runtime
The method runs twice as slow
The method requires items to be mutable
questions.explanation: Because Java generics are invariant, List<Dog> is not a List<Animal>. Declaring Iterable<? extends T> makes the input source covariant, allowing List<Dog> to be passed to a method expecting Animal.

questions.question: In what scenario is ACCUMULATE mode preferred over FAIL_FAST mode in rule validation?
options: When processing real-time network packets where latency is paramount
When validating user form inputs or compliance audits where the caller needs a complete list of all validation errors at once
questions.explanation: ACCUMULATE evaluates all rules and collects every violation, allowing users to see and fix all input errors in a single submission instead of fixing one error at a time.

activities.title: Principal Architect Generics Interview Questions
activities.description: Staff-level design problems on type erasure, wildcards, and high-throughput pipelines.

questions.question: Explain the difference between List<? extends Number> and List<? super Integer> in terms of reading and writing.
questions.answer:
1. List<? extends Number>: Covariant producer. You can safely READ elements from it, and they will be guaranteed to be instances of Number (or its subclasses). However, you CANNOT write any element into it (except null) because the compiler doesn't know the exact concrete subtype (it could be a List<Double> or List<Long>).
2. List<? super Integer>: Contravariant consumer. You can safely WRITE Integer (and its subclasses) into it because it points to an Integer, Number, or Object list. However, when READING from it, elements can only be typed as Object because the list might be a List<Object>.

questions.question: How do you preserve type safety in a heterogeneous container like a pipeline registry without unchecked warnings?
questions.answer: Use the Typesafe Heterogeneous Container pattern: map Class<T> tokens to instances (Map<Class<?>, Object>). Provide a generic method <T> void register(Class<T> type, T instance) and <T> T get(Class<T> type) using type.cast(storage.get(type)). Because the Class<T> token carries runtime type information, the cast is guaranteed to be safe and eliminates raw type warnings.

activities.title: Generic Pipeline Mastery Checklist
activities.description: Verify your readiness to design type-safe generic frameworks.
items: I know when to use <? extends T> (producers/inputs) and <? super T> (consumers/predicates).
I understand why generics are invariant and how wildcards restore covariance and contravariance.
I can implement fluent method chaining with generic builder return types.
I can design execution strategies supporting both FAIL_FAST and ACCUMULATE modes.
I protect pipeline output by returning immutable collections via List.copyOf().

practiceProblems.title: Contravariant Predicate Filter
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement `<T> List<T> filterList(List<T> source, Predicate<? super T> condition)` that evaluates `condition` on each element of `source` and returns an unmodifiable List of matching elements using `List.copyOf()`.

practiceProblems.title: Covariant Producer Transformer
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement `<T, R> List<R> transformAll(Iterable<? extends T> producer, Function<? super T, ? extends R> mapper)` that maps each item in `producer` into type `R` and returns an unmodifiable List.

practiceProblems.title: Composite Rule Evaluator
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement `boolean evaluateAllRules(T item, List<Predicate<? super T>> rules)` that returns `true` if and only if `item` satisfies every predicate in `rules`. If rules is empty, return `true`.

practiceProblems.title: Batch Stream Quarantine Filter
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement `void partitionItems(List<T> source, Predicate<? super T> validator, List<T> passed, List<T> quarantined)` that routes valid items into `passed` and invalid items into `quarantined`.

practiceProblems.title: Safe Bounded Collection Extractor
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement `<T extends Comparable<? super T>> T findMaxItem(Iterable<? extends T> items)` that finds and returns the maximum element using natural ordering. If items is empty or null, return `null`.
